Isaiah was called to his prophetic ministry "in the year that King Uzziah died" (6:1), around 740 b.c. He lived long enough to record the death of Sennacherib (37:38), in 681. However, most of the book can be dated only in very general terms because few specific dates are given.

The central theme of the book is God himself, who does all things for his own glory (48:11). Isaiah defines everything else by how it relates to God: is it rightly related to him as the center of all reality (45:22-25)? God's people find strength only as they rest in the promises of their God (30:15). They find refreshment only as they delight themselves in his word (55:1-2). To serve his cause is their worthy devotion (ch. 62), but to rebel against him is endless death (66:24).

The prophecies of Isaiah took place during the rise of the Assyrian Empire. Assyria posed a great threat to Israel and Judah as well as the entire Near East.
chapter_intro: Encouragement for God’s Exiles: “The Glory of the Lord Shall Be Revealed.”

passages.title: Encouragement for God’s Exiles: “The Glory of the Lord Shall Be Revealed.”
passages.text: These visionary chapters are addressed to the exiles in Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 b.c. (see 39:5–7). Isaiah assures the exiles of God’s care for them. These chapters also address Isaiah’s times by giving long-term hope of the Messiah’s coming.

notes.text: The trusting servant of the Lord will save his despairing people with a salvation available for the whole world.
The servant of the Lord will restore Israel and save the nations. This is the second of four Servant Songs, describing the Messiah (see note on 42:1–9).
O coastlands . . . you peoples from afar. More nations are claimed by God’s grace. He named my name shows God’s personal care for his servant (see 43:1; 45:3–4).
God alone prepared and equipped the servant. my mouth like a sharp sword. Unlike Cyrus, the servant conquers by the truth of his word (see 11:4; Rev. 19:15, 21).
my servant, Israel. Comparing vv. 5–6, this servant Israel restores the nation Israel. The servant is the true embodiment of what the nation failed to be, namely, the one in whom I will be glorified.

It is too light a thing. It is too small a task to redeem only the tribes of Jacob (ethnic Israel). It is clear here that the servant, though he embodies Israel (v. 3), is nevertheless distinct from Israel. He has a calling to serve Israel and beyond. that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. A clear statement of salvation’s worldwide scope, a theme that Acts develops by quoting this text (see Acts 1:8; 13:47).
Unlike the kings of this world, the servant of the Lord conquers by his sufferings (see 50:6; 52:14–15).
The servant’s triumph inspires great joy (see 44:23; 55:12–13; Rom. 8:19–21).
The Lord is more attentive to his people than a mother is to her child.
God moves history for the benefit of his people (see 45:14; 60:10–14).

The people’s skeptical question in v. 24 is answered by the Lord’s strong assertion in vv. 25–26. His people’s enemies will eat their own flesh . . . be drunk with their own blood, as if under siege conditions. Then all flesh shall know that I am the Lord. This is God’s ultimate purpose. This phrase (“all flesh shall know”) comes from Ex. 6:7 and 14:18. It occurs elsewhere in Isaiah (e.g., Isa. 37:20; 45:3; 6; 49:23; 60:16).
